raw_case_text:
A 3-year-old male child resident of Gorakhpur was admitted with complaints of fever for 12 days which was high grade, convulsions (generalized tonic clonic) for 6 days and altered sensorium for 1 day. Examination revealed a febrile child with temperature of 103  F, pulse of 158/min which was feeble, RR of 54/min, blood pressure of 56/32 mm Hg, and Glasgow coma score of 4. Systemic examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly, bilateral rhonchi in chest, tachypnea, tachycardia, extensor planters, and diminished deep tendon reflexes. Investigation of the patient revealed hemoglobin of 9.5 g%, normal cell count and platelet count of 1.8 lakh/ mm3, SGPT of 109 U/ll, urea of 87 mg% and blood glucose of 50 mg%. The CSF study showed a total cell count of 68 cells/ mm3 with 72% lymphocytes and CSF protein of 68 mg% with normal sugar level. As the patient was having long duration of fever with hepatosplenomegaly a clinical suspicion of cerebral malaria as a cause of febrile encephalopathy was made and a rapid diagnostic test for malarial parasites was performed which was positive for both P.vivax and P.falciparum. Peripheral blood smear, both thick and thin film, was sent which showed the presence of both P.vivax and P.falciparum (parasitic count of 6%) [Figure 1]. The Widal test and viral markers for acute hepatitis were negative and blood cultures were sterile. X-ray chest showed right-sided heterogeneous lung opacities and CT scan head done on the third day was normal. The patient was put on a 7-day course of intravenous quinine and doxycycline. However, fever of the patient persisted even on day 8 of admission. Repeat peripheral smear on day 7 of antimalarial treatment was negative for malarial parasite. As the patient was from a JE endemic area (Gorakhpur) and hepatosplenomegaly with deranged renal functions can also occur in JEV encephalitis, a differential diagnosis of JEV encephalitis was kept in mind and CSF of the patient was sent for a virological study. The CSF sample was tested for the presence of IgM antibodies to JEV. CSF was subjected to reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) for detection of entero virus genome and JE virus genome. Serum samples were tested for rise in antibody titer for Coxsackie virus, Enterovirus 76, West Nile virus, and JE virus. CSF of the patient showed only the presence of JE IgM in CSF which confirmed JEV encephalitis in our patient. All other virological tests showed negative results.
The patient was managed symptomatically, shock was treated with ionotropes following which shock improved, and phenytoin was given for seizures and primaquine for radical cure. The child started improving and by the 13th day, fever subsided, blood urea became normal, GCS improved to 12, and repeat peripheral blood smear was negative for malaria parasite. The patient was discharged on day 28 of admission without any sequel. The patient is well on follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 3-year-old male child from Gorakhpur, India, presented with a 12-day history of high-grade fever, 6 days of generalized tonic-clonic convulsions, and 1 day of altered sensorium.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The child experienced 12 days of high-grade fever, followed by generalized tonic-clonic seizures for 6 days and coma/altered sensorium for 1 day prior to admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident of Gorakhpur, India (an endemic region for both malaria and Japanese encephalitis).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high-grade fever, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and coma/altered sensorium.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile (103 F), feeble pulse 158/min, RR 54/min, hypotensive (BP 56/32 mmHg), and comatose with Glasgow Coma Scale score of 4. Systemic exam showed bilateral chest rhonchi, hepatosplenomegaly, diminished deep tendon reflexes, and bilateral extensor plantar responses.
objective.routine_investigations: Hb 9.5 g/dL, normal leukocyte count, platelets 1.8 lakh/mm3, SGPT/ALT 109 U/L, blood urea 87 mg/dL, and hypoglycemia (blood glucose 50 mg/dL). Widal test, viral hepatitis markers, and bacterial blood cultures were negative. Chest X-ray showed right-sided heterogeneous lung opacities.
objective.advanced_workup: Day 3 head CT scan was normal. Lumbar puncture CSF analysis showed lymphocytic pleocytosis (68 cells/mm3, 72% lymphocytes), elevated protein (68 mg/dL), normal glucose, and positive CSF Japanese Encephalitis Virus (JEV) IgM antibodies (CSF enterovirus/JEV RT-PCR and serum viral titers for Coxsackie, Enterovirus 76, and West Nile virus were negative).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Triple co-infection with Plasmodium falciparum malaria, Plasmodium vivax malaria, and Japanese Encephalitis Virus (JEV) meningoencephalitis presenting with febrile coma and shock. Confirmed by positive bivalent malaria rapid diagnostic test, thick and thin blood smears showing both P. vivax and P. falciparum (6% parasitemia), and positive CSF JEV IgM. Treated with a 7-day course of IV quinine and doxycycline (clearing blood smears by day 7), primaquine for radical cure, inotropes for shock, and phenytoin for seizures; fever resolved and GCS improved to 12 by day 13, and he was discharged without neurological sequelae on day 28.
